# A LIST INDEX IS A STRING KEY, LIKE ANY OTHER.
# The defect these rows were written for was in the removed `.$KEY`: at a
# list position TypeScript built a StringVal whose peg was the JS NUMBER
# 0 -- an ill-formed value, not a design choice, since it canoned as a
# bare 0, generated a JSON number, satisfied `number` and failed
# `string`, while Go stringified and was right. The rows are kept under
# `key()`, which agreed with Go throughout, so that the property they
# assert -- an index is a STRING -- stays pinned after the spelling that
# broke it is gone. The `&number` row is the one that does the work.
key-index-gens
key-index-canon
key-index-is-string-canon
key-index-not-number-errc
key-index-per-element-gens
key-nested-list-index-gens
# `key()` IS LATE-BOUND: IT ANSWERS WHERE A VALUE LANDS, NOT WHERE IT
# WAS WRITTEN. A reference COPIES the subtree, and an unresolved key()
# inside the copy resolves at the destination -- `$.a` read into `b.c`
# gives "c", not "a". Same rule that makes key() work under move() and
# inside a spread template, reaching a plain reference too.
# This is the row ADR-009 needs. The removed `.$KEY` was EARLY-bound and
# answered "a" here, so a document rewritten from one spelling to the
# other changes value in exactly this shape (use-cases/BUGS.md §51) --
# from the key of the definition to the key of the use, which is the
# answer G8 phase 1 specified. Written down so the change is a pinned
# rule rather than a surprise.
key-under-a-reference-answers-at-the-destination
key-under-a-type-answers-at-the-use
# A NUMERIC PATH SEGMENT IS A PLAIN DECIMAL INTEGER. NOTHING ELSE IS.
# `$.a.1` is a numeric segment: it indexes a list and addresses the key
# "1". Every other numeric spelling -- hex, `0d`, `_` separators, an
# exponent -- is a STRING KEY spelled exactly as written, because that is
# what those spellings already produce on the KEY side: `a:{0x0:1}`
# generates {"0x0":1}, not {"0":1}. A path spelled like the key it
# addresses is the whole point.
# Both ports were wrong, in opposite directions. TypeScript pushed the
# source text (right) but had no branch at all for the two exact leaves,
# so a `0d` segment was SILENTLY DROPPED and the reference resolved to its
# own CONTAINER -- a wrong value, not a miss. Go normalised every spelling
# to its numeric value, so `$.a.0x0` addressed "0" and `$.a.1e2` addressed
# Each pair is deliberately a hit and a miss: a single row would pass in
# whichever port happens to agree by accident.
path-seg-decimal-list-index
path-seg-decimal-key
path-seg-hex-is-text
path-seg-hex-not-value-err
path-seg-hex-not-index-err
path-seg-exact-is-text
path-seg-exact-not-value-err
path-seg-exact-not-index-err
path-seg-sep-is-text
path-seg-sep-not-value-err
path-seg-exponent-is-text
path-seg-exponent-not-value-err
# In a PATH the dot is always the separator, never a decimal point, which
# is why a float segment splits: `$.a.1.0` is the two plain-decimal
# segments `1` and `0`, and that is how a nested list index is written.
# The split is the reason `1.0` reaches a[1][0] rather than looking for a
# key spelled "1.0", and a future change to segment matching must not
# quietly undo it.
path-seg-nested-list-index
path-seg-nested-list-index-other
path-seg-nested-map-numeric-key
# AN UNSPELLABLE SEGMENT MISSES LOUDLY, IN BOTH PORTS.
# A reference operand no spelling can produce (a boolean, null, a list,
# a map) appends a segment no key can contain (NUL-prefixed), so the
# path can never resolve and the reference reports as unresolved. Go
# used to DROP the segment instead, leaving `**.true` an EMPTY prefix
# path that resolved to its own container -- a PrefVal whose peg was
# itself, and an unrecoverable stack overflow in PrefVal.Canon
# (go/pref.go). TypeScript closed the same hole for the exact number
# leaves (UNSPELLABLE_SEGMENT, ts/src/val/RefVal.ts); these rows pin the
# whole operand family in both engines, at every position: find
# reports the miss where the segment is read, so the code is the same
# at the root as it is nested.
# A LIST INDEX IS CANONICAL DECIMAL, the spelling JavaScript array
# indexing gives the canonical port for free and the Go port now
# spells out (listIndex, go/ref.go): no sign, no leading zeros, and a
# digit run that overflows an index is not one. `vet --at` takes the
# same segments (test/spec/vet.tsv).
ref-list-index
ref-list-index-zero
ref-list-index-leading-zero
ref-list-index-padded
ref-list-index-overflow
ref-list-index-out-of-range
ref-unspellable-bool

# key with an escaped NUL, so matching the marker against real keys
# would trade the silent path-shortening it exists to prevent for a
# different silent wrong value: before find refused it up front, this
# source resolved $.a.true to 7. (The source needs a real NUL, which a
# .tsv cell cannot carry -- the runners' unescape maps \u to u -- so it
